items.title: Secret scanning detects secrets in GitHub Actions workflow logs
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub secret scanning now detects secrets in GitHub Actions workflow logs, in addition to issues, wikis, discussions, and pull requests. Actions workflow log scanning is available in public preview. How does Actions workflow log scanning work? When a workflow run completes, GitHub scans its logs for provider patterns. Findings appear in your repository’s secret scanning alert list, alongside alerts from code and other content, with a link back to the Actions workflow log. Validity checks run for supported secret types, and alerts remain available even after the logs are deleted. How do I enable it? The preview is available to enterprises on GitHub Enterprise Cloud with GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Advanced Security, including those with data residency on GHE.com. Enterprise owners can enable Secret scanning for Actions workflow logs by opening their enterprise settings and selecting Policies, then Advanced Security. Select Enabled in the All repositories dropdown. The policy is disabled by default and applies only to repositories with secret scanning enabled under those licenses. What should I know about the preview? Only workflow runs that complete after you enable the feature are scanned; existing logs aren’t backfilled. Generic patterns, custom patterns, AI-detected secrets, and secrets already masked by Actions aren’t detected. Alerts from Actions workflow logs don’t generate notifications during the preview, so check your repository’s secret scanning alert list directly. Learn more Learn more about secret scanning in our product documentation. Have feedback? Let us know by joining the discussion. We’re listening. The post Secret scanning detects secrets in GitHub Actions workflow logs appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company. In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue. What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the score. Coding. In a simulated file-access task, the team can inspect which files an agent read, whether it checked the copies, and what it did to the shell history afterward. A transcript of the agent’s final reply would miss most of what Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka are evaluating. items.title: AI is destroying my CS degree
items.excerpt: My comment on AI is destroying my CS degree — Hacker News.I don't envy educators right now. AI clearly means you need to change how you teach and evaluate students. We are only a few years in though, and it's still extremely unclear what effective teaching with these tools looks like. The worst part is that the evaluation loop is measured in multiple years! If you start trying some new education mechanism today you won't get a robust idea of how well it works until your current cohort graduate in 3-6 years time. Students effectively all become guinea pigs for untested new ways of learning and teaching. Tags: education, hacker-news, ai, ai-ethics

items.title: Terry Pratchett's Study
items.excerpt: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News.Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) Tags: hacker-news, terry-pratchett

items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.excerpt:
Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML
elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this:
Claude Opus 5.5

The hook

Plugins implement register_agent_reference_types(datasette)...

is supported in GitHub Markdown. You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests

items.title: Claude Mythos 5.2 predicts the structure of a therapy capsid
items.author: Claude
items.excerpt: Claude Mythos 5.2 predicted the structure of a whole AAV capsid, the protein shell used to deliver gene therapies. The capsid is 60 copies of one protein chain. Claude wrote code that runs open-source folding models on overlapping groups of five neighboring chains, then uses the capsid’s symmetry to stitch all 60 together. On AAV2, its prediction landed within about the width of an atom of the experimental structure. Learn more: https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2
